blocks.text: When tomatoes cost ₦300 a basket in Mile 12 market, buyers fill two baskets. When the price climbs to ₦3,000 in the dry season, the same buyers manage half a basket and stretch it with paste. Nobody had to teach them the law of demand.

blocks.markdown:
**Demand** is the quantity of a commodity that consumers are *willing and able* to buy at a given price, over a given period of time.

Both conditions matter. Wanting a car you cannot pay for is desire, not demand. Being able to pay for something you do not want is not demand either. Demand is desire backed by purchasing power and expressed at a stated price.

blocks.title: Law of demand
blocks.text: Other things being equal (ceteris paribus), the higher the price of a commodity, the lower the quantity demanded; and the lower the price, the higher the quantity demanded. Price and quantity demanded therefore move in opposite directions.

blocks.caption: A demand schedule for tomatoes. Plotting price on the vertical axis against quantity on the horizontal axis gives a demand curve sloping downwards from left to right

blocks.markdown:
### Why the demand curve slopes downwards

Three reasons work together. First, the **income effect**: a price fall leaves the consumer with more real purchasing power, so more can be bought. Second, the **substitution effect**: when tomatoes become dearer, buyers switch to pepper, paste or dried tomato. Third, **diminishing marginal utility**: each extra basket gives less satisfaction than the one before, so a buyer will only take more if the price falls.

### Change in quantity demanded versus change in demand

This distinction earns marks every year, so keep it sharp.

A **change in quantity demanded** is caused by a change in the commodity's *own price*. The consumer moves from one point to another **along the same demand curve** — an extension of demand when price falls, a contraction when price rises.

A **change in demand** is caused by any factor *other than* price. The **whole curve shifts**: to the right for an increase in demand, to the left for a decrease. Those other factors are:

- consumer income
- the price of substitutes and complements
- taste, fashion and advertising
- the size and structure of the population
- expectations of future price changes
- season and weather
- government policy, such as a ban or a tax on the good

rows: A good wanted for several different uses
Maize demanded for pap, for animal feed and for industrial starch
Goods that are substitutes for one another
Rice and spaghetti; Peak milk and Dano milk
Goods demanded together because one is useless without the other
Cars and petrol; bread and butter; phones and data bundles
A good demanded not for itself but for what it helps produce
Cement demanded because houses are demanded; labour demanded because output is demanded
A good demanded for immediate personal satisfaction
blocks.caption: Types of demand with Nigerian examples

items: **Goods of ostentation (Veblen goods)** — designer bags, luxury cars and jewellery may be bought *more* as price rises, because the high price is the point.
**Expectation of further price rises** — if buyers expect the price of cement to keep climbing, a price increase today can trigger panic buying.
**Price taken as a signal of quality** — some buyers assume the cheaper drug is fake and buy more of the dearer one.
**Giffen goods** — a very inferior staple whose price fall makes consumers so much better off that they switch part of their spending to a superior food and buy less of the staple.
**Emergencies and necessities** — a sick person will buy the prescribed medicine at almost any price.

blocks.title: Deciding whether the curve shifts or you move along it
blocks.prompt: For each event, state whether it causes a change in quantity demanded for beef or a change in demand for beef, and in which direction: (i) the price of beef falls from ₦4,000 to ₦3,200 per kg; (ii) the minimum wage is raised; (iii) the price of chicken, a substitute, falls sharply.

steps.text: Ask one question first: did the price of BEEF ITSELF change? If yes, you move along the curve. If no, the curve shifts.
(i) The price of beef itself fell, so this is a change in quantity demanded — an extension of demand. The buyer moves down along the same demand curve.
(ii) A higher minimum wage raises income, not the price of beef, so the whole curve shifts. Beef is a normal good, so demand increases and the curve shifts to the right.
(iii) The price of a substitute changed, not the price of beef, so the curve shifts. Buyers switch to the cheaper chicken, so demand for beef decreases and the curve shifts to the left.
Summarise the rule: own price means movement along; anything else means a shift.

blocks.answer: (i) extension of demand, a movement along the curve; (ii) increase in demand, rightward shift; (iii) decrease in demand, leftward shift

blocks.title: Wording matters
blocks.text: Use the phrases the examiner expects. Price changes give an *extension* or *contraction* of demand; non-price factors give an *increase* or *decrease* in demand. Candidates who write "demand increased because price fell" lose the mark even when they understand the economics.

points: Demand is the quantity consumers are willing and able to buy at a given price in a given period.
The law of demand: price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions, ceteris paribus.
The demand curve slopes downwards because of the income effect, the substitution effect and diminishing marginal utility.
A change in the good's own price moves you along the curve; any other factor shifts the whole curve.
Types of demand include composite, competitive, complementary, derived and direct demand.
Exceptions to the law include goods of ostentation, expected further price rises, price as a quality signal and Giffen goods.
